c.tagline: Hills tumble to Atlantic beaches in West Africa's most storied harbor city.

taxi.fareNote: Shared taxis run fixed routes for a small fixed fare; private/charter taxis must be negotiated before the ride as meters are not used.

emergency.note: Emergency response is unreliable outside central Freetown; private hospitals (e.g., Choithram Memorial) and travel insurance with medevac are strongly recommended.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Avoid the Kroo Bay and Susan's Bay slum areas, and downtown streets or beaches after dark.
Pickpocketing is common in crowded markets around Sani Abacha Street; use trusted drivers rather than street taxis at night.

hood_desc: Freetown's main expat and tourist hub near the beach with the widest choice of hotels, restaurants and bars; good base for water-taxi arrivals and nightlife.
Long sandy beach strip lined with beach bars, seafood shacks and mid-range hotels; best for travelers who want beach access and a laid-back vibe close to Aberdeen.
A quiet, leafy hillside area with colonial-era buildings and NGO/diplomatic residences; suits travelers wanting calm, greenery and views over the city and harbor.
Central residential-commercial districts with local markets, offices and mid-range guesthouses; convenient for business travelers wanting proximity to downtown without full city chaos.
The historic commercial core with the Cotton Tree, government buildings, markets and colonial architecture; suits budget travelers and those focused on history and city sightseeing.

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; use bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Poda podas, kekes and okadas are paid in cash directly to the driver/conductor in leones, with fares agreed or fixed by route; there is no electronic fare card system. Water taxis and ferries are booked and paid at the terminal or online in advance.
transit.hours: Poda podas and shared taxis run roughly 6am-9pm; okadas and kekes operate later into the evening; official night options are limited so pre-arranged transport is safer after dark.
transit.note: Traffic congestion is severe, especially around Congo Cross and central Freetown during peak hours.

bus: Freetown City Council public bus network

airport.name: Freetown Lungi International Airport (FNA)
airport.drive: The airport sits across the estuary from the city; direct road drive is 4-5 hrs via Port Loko, so almost all travelers use a boat/ferry crossing plus a short taxi instead.

transit.m: Sea Coach Express water taxi to Aberdeen/Government Wharf (~35-45 min)
Seabird Express speedboat to Aberdeen (~30-40 min)
Hovercraft/ferry option (when running) to Government Wharf (~45 min)
Road transfer via Port Loko/Petifu bridge road (4-5 hrs)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or 5-10% at upscale restaurants and hotels is appreciated but not expected at local eateries.

food.name: Cassava leaf plasas
food.desc: Sierra Leone's national dish: pounded cassava leaves simmered slowly in red palm oil with smoked fish, beef and pepper, spooned over white rice.

places.name: Papaya Restaurant
places.note: Known for big-portion, boldly seasoned Sierra Leonean plates including cassava leaf.

places.name: Mama Yema's Restaurant
places.note: Home-style kitchen with a menu built on Sierra Leonean soups and stews.

places.name: B'Classic Kitchen
places.note: Straight-down-the-line local cooking; the plasas is the plate to order.

food.name: Jollof rice
food.desc: Rice cooked down in a tomato, onion and pepper base until it takes on colour and a little smoky crust at the bottom of the pot, served with chicken or fish.

places.name: Papaya Restaurant
places.note: Reliable and generous version alongside fried plantain.

places.name: Lily's Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Local and international menu with a solid jollof, near the beach strip.

places.name: Bliss Restaurant
places.note: Garden setting that fills up evenings and weekends; mixed local and international menu.

food.name: Fried fish with pepper sauce
food.desc: Whole snapper or barracuda scored, fried or grilled over coals, and served with a fierce scotch bonnet pepper sauce, fried plantain and rice.

places.name: Lumley Beach grills
places.note: Informal beach shacks grilling the day's catch to order as the sun goes down.

places.name: The Lighthouse Restaurant
places.note: Hilltop seafood specialist with ocean views; prawns and lobster too.

places.name: Roy's Beach Bar
places.note: Long-running beachfront bar and grill, popular for fish and cold drinks.

food.name: Groundnut soup
food.desc: Peanut-thickened stew with beef or chicken, tomato and chilli, poured over rice. Rich, nutty and one of the most-loved everyday Sierra Leonean plates.

places.name: Mama Yema's Restaurant
places.note: Hearty home cooking with the classic soups done properly.

places.name: B'Classic Kitchen
places.note: Authentic Sierra Leonean menu with a rotating soup of the day.

places.name: Big Market cookery stalls
places.note: Market cook shops ladling soups over rice at local prices; busiest stall is the best.

food.name: Krain krain with fufu
food.desc: Slippery jute-leaf stew cooked with palm oil, fish and hot pepper, eaten with cassava fufu or foofoo rolled by hand. Earthy and unmistakably West African.

places.name: B'Classic Kitchen
places.note: Traditional leaf soups served with fufu the way locals eat them.

places.name: Big Market cookery stalls
places.note: Cheapest and most authentic option; point at the pot you want.

places.name: Mama Yema's Restaurant
places.note: Comfortable sit-down setting if you would rather not eat standing in the market.

food.name: Akara and street fry fry
food.desc: Black-eyed pea fritters fried golden and eaten hot with pepper, sold alongside roast plantain, fried fish and meat pies from morning street stands.

places.name: Congo Cross street vendors
places.note: Busy junction with fryers going from breakfast; cheap and quick.

places.name: Big Market area vendors
places.note: Dense run of snack sellers around the market and Wallace Johnson Street.

places.name: Crown Bakery
places.note: Long-established Freetown bakery for meat pies and pastries if you want a sit-down snack.

food.name: Ginger beer
food.desc: Home-brewed ginger steeped with lime and sugar until it burns the throat, sold ice cold in bottles and sachets. Freetown's non-alcoholic drink of choice.

places.name: Big Market area vendors
places.note: Home-made bottles chilled in coolers; the strongest and cheapest version.

places.name: Congo Cross street vendors
places.note: Roadside sellers with ginger beer and bissap sorrel in frozen sachets.

places.name: Papaya Restaurant
places.note: Restaurant version served over ice, milder if you want to ease in.

food.name: Star lager
food.desc: Sierra Leone's own beer, brewed in Freetown and drunk very cold on the beach. Bars also pour poyo, the tart fresh palm wine tapped upcountry.

places.name: Roy's Beach Bar
places.note: Beachfront institution for a cold Star with grilled fish at sunset.

places.name: The Lighthouse Restaurant
places.note: Hilltop drinks with sea views before dinner.

places.name: Bliss Restaurant
places.note: Relaxed garden bar that gets going in the evenings.

landmarks: Cotton Tree
This towering, centuries-old kapok tree in the city center is Freetown's most famous symbol, linked to the legend of freed slaves who settled here in 1792.
Sierra Leone National Museum
Located beside the Cotton Tree, this museum showcases the nation's history and culture through artifacts, masks, and colonial-era relics.
State House
The seat of Sierra Leone's government, this stately hilltop building is a striking example of the city's colonial and post-independence architecture.
St. George's Cathedral
A 19th-century Anglican cathedral built partly from stones salvaged from slave ships, standing as a poignant reminder of Freetown's founding history.
Fourah Bay College
Founded in 1827, this historic institution was the first Western-style university in Sub-Saharan Africa, earning Freetown the nickname 'Athens of West Africa.'
Fort Thornton
This hilltop colonial fort and residence offers commanding views over Freetown's harbor and skyline, steeped in the city's founding-era history.
Bunce Island
A haunting former slave-trading outpost upriver from Freetown, its ruined fortifications make for a somber but essential historical pilgrimage.
Lakka Beach
A palm-fringed stretch of golden sand just outside the capital, popular with locals and visitors for swimming, relaxing, and fresh seafood.
King Jimmy Market
A chaotic, colorful waterfront market where vendors sell everything from fish to fabrics, offering an authentic slice of everyday Freetown life.
Big Market
A historic covered marketplace in downtown Freetown known for wood carvings, textiles, and handmade crafts sold under its distinctive colonial-era roof.

train.note: No passenger railway. The old Sierra Leone Government Railway closed in the 1970s and the remaining mineral lines are freight only. Travel overland is by road (bus and shared taxi).

bus.note: ST Transport runs a long-distance West-Africa coach; it has no proper booking website, only a Facebook page, so confirm departures by phone/in person. The everyday way to reach Conakry (Guinea) or Monrovia (Liberia) is shared bush taxis toward the Gbalamuya/Kambia and Bo-Waterside borders - carry Guinea/Liberia visas and ECOWAS vehicle papers.

ferry.note: No international passenger ferries. The main local boat is the domestic Freetown water-taxi/ferry across the estuary to Lungi (for the international airport) - handy, but not a long-distance route.
